question: None shared. Both are clinician practice surveys, and the populations surveyed are different classes of clinician in different health systems: 50 high-volume US psychiatrists from an opt-in panel (P-1017) and 121 Italian neurologists at board-selected MCI centres (P-1080), which excluded psychiatrists. The recorded disagreement sets P-1017's favourable conclusion ('can provide timely and accurate diagnosis') against P-1080's unfavourable one ('suboptimal management'). Both are authors' verdicts about different clinicians, not a measured clinical quantity.
metric: No shared metric for the verdicts. The measured quantities are proportions of different units and items: share of a psychiatrist's own caseload personally diagnosed, and share of psychiatrists using a method, against share of neurologists or of their patients with a given criterion, test or treatment.

figures.P-1017: Mental status testing 94% of 50 psychiatrists (47/50; Wilson 0.838-0.979); diagnostic imaging 55% (Wilson 0.413-0.679); blood testing 59% (0.452-0.715). All self-reported.
figures.P-1080: MMSE used for screening by 93.3% of 121 neurologists (Wilson 0.874-0.966); brain MRI recommended by 97.5% (0.929-0.991); routine laboratory tests performed by 'almost the totality'. All phase-1 self-reports.
figures.comparison: On the one item both surveys ask, use of a brief mental-status screen, the proportions agree (94% against 93.3%; each inside the other's interval). The imaging and laboratory items differ beyond uncertainty (55% against 97.5%), but they compare psychiatrists with neurologists in two countries, using different item wording ('utilizing ... diagnostic imaging' to make the diagnosis against 'recommend brain MRI'). Neither paper claims the other's figure is wrong.

matched_figure_check: The one matched item (brief cognitive screening) agrees. Neither paper reports the other's clinician population: P-1080 surveyed neurologists only, and P-1017's specialty breakdown of methods is for psychiatrists.
reason: The recorded conflict sets two authors' verdicts about different clinician populations against each other: US psychiatrists' self-reported diagnostic role against Italian neurologists' heterogeneous practice. Neither verdict is a measured quantity. Where the two surveys ask the same question (use of a brief mental-status screen), they agree, 94% against 93.3%. The items that differ numerically compare different specialties, countries and item wordings, so they fail the same-question condition.
